### Introducing Polyvox

I’m happy to share that the Polyvox app is now available for iOS and Android!

Polyvox is an app for learning foreign languages (for now, just Mandarin Chinese), by speaking and listening with a digital 3D teacher.

This is 刘子枫 (Liu Zifeng), the first teacher available in the app.

Liu Zifeng will take you through a series of lessons designed for early and intermediate Mandarin Chinese learners — all in 100% native Chinese.

You’ll talk back to her through the microphone on your device. Don’t worry if you’re learning Chinese for the first time, the app uses very tolerant speech recognition to accommodate beginner accents.

## Is it an AI language learning app?

Kind of, but not really.

There’s a plethora of AI language learning products on the market at the moment, most built on Large Language Models APIs (LLMs, a type of text-based AI model) that take on the persona of a foreign language teacher.

There is definitely a place for these, but there are a couple of problems.

First, they can’t (yet) run on mobile devices, so all of these products require an internet connection and a monthly or yearly subscription. If your subscription lapses or the company goes under, you’re left with nothing.

## Intro

Heard recently about BFF. I have used it before, however, I like when people, become enthusiastic about a technology. It is so interesting almost funny, it also drives the incentive to discover it more.

I have refreshed myself on the topic, read a couple of articles and spotted a pattern. This article is about the dissonance I am feeling, after I used BFF, with what is being written about it, and what can be truly beneficial about it, in my opinion.

## A little bit about the name

"Backend For Frontend" - if you call it this way you follow the usage coined by Phil Calçado PhilCalcado.com- BEFFE, however, it was shrunk to BFF by Nick Fisher. I think Phil Calçado is the first who described this pattern, though.

"Backend For Frontends" - if you call it this way you follow the usage promoted by Sam Newman SamNewman.io who adds some additional flavors to it.

## Description

As PhilCalcado.com describes, it is a pattern that facilitates communication between FE with only one BE. For example segregated between Web and Mobile, you have one Mobile FE communicating with Mobile BFF, similarly for Web.

However, how it is used in reality or at least how I have seen it used, is that each domain be that, invoice, order, bill, contracts, etc. has it's own BFF. This is closer to how Sam Newman describes it SamNewman.io, however, at an even more granular level.

# The Simple Math Behind Why Stocks Must Increase More After Declines

2 min read

Apr 13, 2025

--

Listen

Share

Investors often underestimate the mathematics behind recovering from losses in the stock market. A 20% drop in a stock’s price doesn’t require a 20% gain to return to the original value. In reality, it requires a significantly larger increase. Here’s the math explained simply, along with Python code and visuals to illustrate clearly.

## The Math Explained

When a stock price declines, it must rise by a larger percentage than it fell to get back to its original level. For example:

- If a stock drops by 20% from $100, its new price is $80.
- To recover to $100 from $80, it must rise by $20, or 25%.

This asymmetry grows exponentially larger with more significant drops.

## Why Does This Happen?

The relationship is due to percentage calculations being based on different starting values for losses and recoveries:

- Percentage loss is calculated from the higher initial price.
- Percentage recovery is calculated from the lower, decreased price.

# Football Field Chart (Fin Analysis)

7 min read

Apr 17, 2025

--

Share

Imagine you want to know how much a stock is worth. Not one answer, but many. Different methods give different values. This Python code helps you see these values clearly, all at once.

First, you enter a stock ticker, like AAPL for Apple. You choose how you want to gather the numbers. You can scrape them from the web, type them in yourself, or load them from a file. Each method has its value range: low, middle, and high.

The code creates something called a football field chart. This chart looks just like a football field — green, with clear lines and goal posts marking the current stock price. Each valuation method is shown as a bar. These bars tell you the low and high values that experts suggest. The middle line on each bar is the best guess.

For example, the P/E ratio method might suggest Apple is worth between $140 and $160, with the best guess at $150. Another technique, EV/EBITDA, might show a slightly different range.

The yellow goal post marks today’s stock price. This helps you quickly see if the stock is undervalued or overpriced compared to all the valuation methods.

# Cadence, Choo Choo!!

7 min read

Jan 27, 2016

--

1

Share

Over the last four years the mobile team at Strava has shipped more than fifty releases across Android and iOS. Our release cycle has varied from over three months for huge monolithic features to less than a week for hotfixes of issues discovered shortly after releasing. Historically app updates and new feature releases have been tightly coupled. As demands on each release escalated we saw release dates slip and quality jump around due to making concessions trying to push a release out the door. After going through a particularly ambitious release in early Spring 2015 we needed to reassess how and when we release.

“The Lumens Express” by Nick Fisher is under CC BY-ND 2.0

At the end of Summer 2015 we shipped a landmark update. The difference between this release and the scores of prior releases was not a groundbreaking feature or an important bug fix, the difference was that this release went out on its own schedule: it was not dictated by the need to release a certain feature and it was not a response to an emergency.
